15.title: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling
15.hook: agape: the word for love that isn't a feeling
15.carry: love is what you do when you don't feel it
15.howItsDone: Christians often read 1 Corinthians 13 at weddings and funerals, and Christian teachers often describe agape as the love God shows first and asks people to show each other, in what they do more than in what they feel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Beatitudes, the list that starts at the bottom. Week three begins with a word everyone thinks they already know.

At a lot of weddings, someone's cousin stands up, a little nervous, and reads: love is patient, love is kind. It's on cards, on mugs, on the wall above somebody's couch. It's so familiar it sounds soft. But it wasn't written for a wedding. It was written to a church that was falling apart: people taking each other to court, splitting into camps behind their favorite teachers, showing off who was more spiritual. Paul had started that church, in the Greek city of Corinth. And in the middle of a letter full of scolding, he stopped and wrote this.
screen: `LOVE IS PATIENT, LOVE IS KIND.` → `NOT WRITTEN FOR A WEDDING.` → `WRITTEN TO A CHURCH IN A FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Love. English has one word for it. You love your mother, your dog, pizza, a song. Greek had several. Eros, the love that wants. Philia, the love between friends. And the one Paul chose here: agape. Christian teachers have long filled it with a particular meaning: love as a choice, not a mood. Love that acts for someone's good whether or not you feel warm about them. Listen to how Paul describes it, in the old English: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Charity. That's the old translation's word, from the Latin caritas, related to the word for dear, even costly. Today charity sounds like a donation box, so newer Bibles say love. But the old word tells you something: this is love with its sleeves rolled up. Notice something else. In Paul's Greek, almost every line in the passage is a verb. Suffers long. Is kind. Doesn't envy. Doesn't brag. He isn't describing a feeling. He's describing behavior, the kind you could watch someone do. That's why it fit a church full of people who didn't like each other. He wasn't asking them to feel warm. He was asking them to be patient and kind, and to stop showing off. He ends: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Christians say this is how God loves first. Another letter puts it simply: "We love him, because he first loved us."
screen: `GREEK HAD SEVERAL WORDS.` · `AGAPE — LOVE AS A CHOICE.` · `CHARITY — LOVE WITH SLEEVES UP.` · `EVERY LINE IS A VERB.` · then, large: `THE GREATEST OF THESE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out slowly. Think of someone who's hard to love right now. Not the hardest person in your life; someone mildly difficult. A coworker. A relative. A roommate. You don't have to feel anything warm. Just picture them, and ask one plain question: what would be kind, for them? Something small and real. Let an answer come, or don't. Then just breathe, and let the question rest.
Love. In Greek, agape: love that's a choice, not a mood. The old English calls it charity. Fifteenth word.
Your line: love is what you do when you don't feel it. Paul wrote it to people who didn't like each other. Week three, begun.

16.title: not certainty
16.hook: not certainty; a mustard seed, and a father who believed and doubted at once
16.howItsDone: Christians describe faith as trust in God, and in times of doubt or dryness some pray the father's line from Mark: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."

segments.voice: Yesterday: love, the kind you do when you don't feel it. Today, a word for the days you don't feel much of anything.

You pray, and feel nothing. You sit in a service where everyone around you seems moved, and wonder what you're missing. Next to people whose faith looks like a wall, solid and never shaken, it's easy to decide faith belongs to other people. Here's a scene from Mark's Gospel. A father brings his son, who has suffered since childhood, and the disciples couldn't help. The father says: if you can do anything, help us. Jesus tells him all things are possible to the one who believes. And the father cries out, in tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once.
screen: `YOU PRAY, AND FEEL NOTHING.` → `A FATHER, OUT OF OPTIONS.` → `"I BELIEVE; HELP MY UNBELIEF."`

segments.voice: Faith. The Greek word is pistis, and it's less about certainty than about trust. It's the word for trusting a friend, or being faithful to one. You have faith in someone the way you have faith in a bridge: not because you've proved it, but because you're willing to put your weight on it. Amen, on day eight, came from a root meaning firm, solid. Same idea. Now, how much of it do you need? Another Gospel tells the same story, and afterward the disciples ask why they couldn't help the boy. Jesus answers: "If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove." He doesn't say: if you had enormous faith. He says: if you had even this much. The mountain is big. The seed is tiny. The point is the seed. A letter in the Bible puts it another way: "faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." Not seen. And not always felt. Mother Teresa's private letters, published after her death, describe years of feeling God's absence when she prayed. She kept praying. And doubt sat in the very first congregation: after Easter, one Gospel says the disciples saw Jesus on a mountain, and "they worshipped him: but some doubted." So some Christian writers have said that doubt, and even dryness, isn't simply faith's opposite. The father in Mark didn't bring a perfect faith. He brought a half-sure, crying, both-at-once faith, and the story doesn't send him away. Jesus heals the boy.
screen: `PISTIS — TRUST, NOT PROOF.` · `A MUSTARD SEED.` · `THINGS NOT SEEN, NOT FELT.` · `DOUBT ISN'T THE OPPOSITE.` · then, large: `SMALL IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If there's something tiny nearby, a grain of rice, a seed, a crumb, put it in your palm. If not, just open your hand. Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you're unsure about. Don't solve it. Just admit it. Now think of one small thing you do trust: the floor holding you up, the next breath coming, one person. Let that small thing be enough, for now. If you pray, the father's words are there for you: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
Faith. Pistis. Not certainty: trust, even the size of a seed. Sixteenth word.
Your line: small is enough. On a day you feel nothing, a seed's worth still counts. Day sixteen.

17.title: David shouting at God
17.hook: David shouting at God — anger is allowed
17.carry: you can say anything to him
17.tomorrow: why the symbol is an execution device
17.howItsDone: Christians sing and pray the Psalms in church services and at home. In monasteries, and in the daily prayer of some churches, the Psalms are prayed in order over a set cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday: faith, and a father who believed and doubted in the same breath. Your line was small is enough. Today, a whole book of honest prayers.

Anger at a person. Anger at a life. Sometimes, anger at God, or the universe, or whoever runs things. It can seem like the one feeling nobody brings to church, where everyone shows up polite. Now open the middle of the Bible, and there's a whole book of people who didn't. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" That's not a complaint about God. It's a complaint to God, out loud, and it's scripture.

The Psalms. A hundred and fifty poems, the songbook of ancient Israel, still prayed by Jews and by Christians. The name comes from Greek, psalmos, a song sung to a plucked string. The Hebrew title is Tehillim: praises. Tradition ties many of them to David, the shepherd boy who became king; the headings put his name on about half, and scholars debate how many he actually wrote. For a book called praises, a great deal of it is complaint. Scholars call these laments, and there are a lot of them. That first line asks how long four times in two verses. Another psalm opens with a cry you'll hear again tomorrow, from the cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" And one psalm ends in darkness, with no comfort at all. If prayer has ever felt like talking to the ceiling, that one is in the book too. These weren't hidden away. Many carry headings addressed to the chief musician: songs to be sung. Laments often have a shape. First the honest part: where are you, this isn't fair, I'm going under. Then, often, a turn. The how long psalm ends by saying the singer has trusted in God's mercy and will sing again. In these songs, the anger doesn't have to be cleaned up first. It's the way in.
screen: `TEHILLIM — PRAISES.` · `SO MUCH OF IT IS COMPLAINT.` · `"HOW LONG?" FOUR TIMES.` · `FIRST THE HONEST PART. THEN A TURN.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T HAVE TO BE POLITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe. Think of something you're upset about. Not a crisis, but something real, something you've been keeping polite about. Silently, say it straight. No softening. How long. Why. This isn't fair. If you pray, you can say it to God, the way the Psalms do. If you don't, say it to the quiet. Then breathe, and notice what's left once it's been said. You don't have to fix anything.
The Psalms. A hundred and fifty songs, with praise and complaint side by side. Seventeenth word.
Your line: you can say anything to him. The Psalms were saying it long before anyone told you to be polite. Day seventeen, done.

18.title: why the symbol is an execution device
18.hook: why the symbol is an execution device
18.carry: the worst thing is not the last thing
18.tomorrow: the women went to the tomb first
18.howItsDone: Christians remember the crucifixion on Good Friday, the Friday before Easter. Catholic, Orthodox and some Protestant Christians make the sign of the cross when they pray, and churches often hold a crucifix or a plain cross at the front.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Psalms, and a cry that opens one of them. Today, the place that cry was heard again. The hardest word in this camp.

On a steeple. On a necklace. Tattooed on a forearm. Hanging from a rearview mirror. The cross is everywhere, and it's easy to stop seeing it. So try a swap. A movement whose symbol was an electric chair. A tiny gold noose on a chain. It sounds unthinkable. But that's what the cross was to the people who first saw it: the way Rome killed the people it wanted everyone to watch die. So why would anyone wear one?
screen: `ON A STEEPLE. ON A NECKLACE.` → `NOW SWAP IN AN ELECTRIC CHAIR.` → `WHY WOULD ANYONE WEAR ONE?`

segments.voice: Crucifixion was how Rome executed slaves, rebels and anyone it saw as a threat to order. It was slow, and it was public on purpose. The Gospels say Jesus was arrested at night, questioned, and handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, who sentenced him. Roman soldiers carried it out. Over his head was written the charge: the King of the Jews. A mockery, and a warning. The Gospels keep a few things he said there. One has him pray: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." In Mark's Gospel he cries out, in his own language, yesterday's line: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" The Gospels don't smooth that over. Some Christian readers say it's there so that anyone who has felt abandoned knows he felt it too. Then a turn in the history. Historians of early Christian art say the oldest surviving images more often show other signs: a fish, an anchor, a shepherd. The cross became the main symbol later, after Rome stopped crucifying people. Christians say something happened there that changed what the worst thing means. Churches put it in different words: a sacrifice, a rescue, love going all the way down. And they show it differently. Catholic and Orthodox churches often show the crucifix, with Jesus on it. Some Protestant churches show the cross empty. Both are saying something about that Friday: it happened, and Christians say it wasn't the end.
screen: `ROME'S PUBLIC EXECUTION.` · `"FATHER, FORGIVE THEM."` · `FIRST A FISH, AN ANCHOR.` · `THE CRUCIFIX AND THE EMPTY CROSS.` · then, large: `IT WASN'T THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out. Think of a hard thing from this year. Not the hardest. Just name it, quietly, without reliving it. Now notice one plain fact: you're still here. Something came after it, even if it's only this minute, sitting and breathing. You don't have to make it mean anything. Just hold both: it happened, and it wasn't the last thing. If you pray, you can bring it with you.
The cross. Rome's execution, turned into the sign on the steeple. Eighteenth word.
Your line: the worst thing is not the last thing. Tomorrow is a Sunday morning, at first light. Day eighteen.

screen: `DAY 18 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WOMEN WENT TO THE TOMB FIRST.`

19.title: the women went to the tomb first
19.hook: the women went to the tomb first
19.howItsDone: Christians celebrate Easter as their greatest feast, often with a vigil the night before or a service at sunrise. Many greet each other with "Christ is risen" and answer "he is risen indeed." Orthodox churches often keep Easter on a later date, by an older calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cross, Rome's execution on a Friday. Your line was the worst thing is not the last thing. Now, the Sunday.
screen: `THE WORST THING IS NOT THE LAST THING.` → `DAY 19.`

segments.voice: It's very early on a Sunday, first light. Three women are walking to a grave, carrying spices. Their friend was executed on Friday, and there wasn't time to prepare his body before the Sabbath, so they're going now. It's the last thing you can do for someone you love. And on the way, they realize they have a problem. The tomb is sealed with a big stone, and none of them can move it. Mark's Gospel keeps the question they ask each other on the road: "Who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulchre?"
screen: `SUNDAY. FIRST LIGHT.` → `THREE WOMEN, CARRYING SPICES.` → `WHO WILL MOVE THE STONE?`

segments.voice: Easter. In most of the world its name comes from Pascha, from the Hebrew word for Passover, because it happened in Passover week. Where the English word Easter comes from, nobody is completely sure. In Mark, the women arrive, and the stone is already rolled back. Inside sits a young man dressed in white, who tells them: "he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him." And the oldest copies of Mark end almost right there. The women run from the tomb, trembling, and say nothing to anyone, "for they were afraid." Fear, and an empty room. Most scholars agree the longer endings in many Bibles were added later, and many churches still read them. Another Gospel tells it closer up. Mary Magdalene comes alone, while it's still dark, and finds the stone gone. She stays outside, crying. A man asks why she's weeping, and she thinks he's the gardener. Then he says one word. Her name. "Mary." And she knows him. Now notice who's there first. Not Peter. Not the twelve. Women, in a world where a woman's word counted for little. Every Gospel puts them at the tomb first. Easter is the center of the Christian year. Christians say Jesus rose from the dead, and that death doesn't get the last word. On Easter morning many greet each other: Christ is risen. And the answer comes back: he is risen indeed.
screen: `PASCHA — FROM PASSOVER.` · `"HE IS RISEN; HE IS NOT HERE."` · `MARY. SHE KNOWS HIM.` · `THE WOMEN WERE THERE FIRST.` · then, large: `THE STONE IS ALREADY MOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe. Think of a stone in your life right now: something heavy in the way, that you've been worrying about on the road before you've even gotten there. Name it. Now, just for this minute, picture walking up and finding it already moved. Don't plan how. Don't argue with it. Just let yourself feel the relief, and breathe into it. If you pray, you can hand the stone over. If you don't, notice how much of the weight was the worrying.
Easter. Pascha. The morning the stone was moved and the tomb was empty. Nineteenth word.
Your line: the stone is already moved. The women worried about it the whole way there. See you tomorrow.

20.title: not a building
20.hook: not a building — the people; the Greek word means "the called-out ones"
20.tomorrow: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead
20.howItsDone: Many Christians gather with a church on Sundays for worship, and many also meet in small groups at home during the week. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches are organized differently, but all speak of the church as the people, not the building.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Easter, and the women at the tomb at first light. Today, what those first witnesses became.

Say the word church and a picture comes up. A steeple. Stained glass. A cathedral so big your voice echoes, or a strip-mall storefront with folding chairs. Everybody pictures a building. But for about the first two hundred years, Christians had almost no church buildings at all. They met in kitchens and courtyards, around somebody's table. Paul ends one of his letters with greetings to a married couple, and adds: "greet the church that is in their house." The church was in the house. Which means it wasn't the house.
screen: `SAY "CHURCH." WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `200 YEARS, ALMOST NO BUILDINGS.` → `"THE CHURCH THAT IS IN THEIR HOUSE."`

segments.voice: The word in the New Testament is Greek: ekklesia. It's made of two small pieces: ek, out, and a word for calling. The called-out ones. In a Greek city, the ekklesia was the assembly: the citizens called out of their homes to gather and decide things together. It wasn't a place. It was people, showing up. So when the first Christians needed a word for themselves, that's the one they picked. Not the temple. Not a sacred site. The gathering. Paul pushes it further. He tells one of his churches: "ye are the body of Christ." Hands, feet, eyes, ears. All different. None of them the whole thing, and none able to say to the others, I don't need you. That's how he pictures a church: not a crowd of the same person, but a body of very different ones. Then the smallest church there is. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus promises: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three. Not two or three hundred. Christians today gather in every size there is. Cathedrals that took centuries to build. House churches still meeting around a kitchen table. A hospital room, a prison, a video call. Churches differ a lot about how they're led and how they're joined. But almost all of them would say this much: the building is where the church meets. The people are the church. Which is why it can hurt so much when they fail you. If a church once hurt you, that's real, and it isn't small. Many Christians would say the people who failed you aren't the whole church, and they aren't Christ.
screen: `EKKLESIA — THE CALLED-OUT ONES.` · `AN ASSEMBLY, NOT A PLACE.` · `"YE ARE THE BODY OF CHRIST."` · `TWO OR THREE.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE ARE THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out slowly. Think of the two or three people you'd call if something went wrong tonight. The ones who'd show up. Picture them, one at a time: their faces, where they are right now. Then widen it a little, to someone who showed up for you once and never knew what it meant. If you pray, you can gather them in your prayer. If you don't, just let them be gathered here with you for a minute.
The church. Ekklesia. Not a building: the called-out ones, gathered. Twentieth word.
Your line: find two or three. That's the smallest church there is, and it counts. Day twenty.

21.title: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead
21.hook: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead; "the beginning of the good news"
21.howItsDone: Christians hear the Gospels read aloud in church, and some churches follow a cycle of readings in which one year draws largely on Mark. Some groups read the whole of Mark aloud in one sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the church, the people, not the building. Now the whole camp, quickly: communion, the Trinity, born again, baptism, testimony, the Holy Spirit, the Bible, amen, grace, Jesus, the Lord's Prayer, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Beatitudes, love, faith, the Psalms, the cross, Easter, the church. Twenty words. Today makes twenty-one.
screen: `FIND TWO OR THREE.` → the strand, twenty words lit.

segments.voice: So many of those words lead back to four short books: the Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. On day seven you heard that a lot of people start reading the Bible with a Gospel. The shortest of the four is Mark. Sixteen chapters. You could read the whole thing aloud in one sitting, in somebody's living room. It's fast. It's blunt. It skips the parts you'd expect. There's no Christmas in it, no shepherds, no star. It starts with a man shouting in the desert. And its very first line is today's word.
screen: `FOUR SHORT BOOKS.` → `MARK: THE SHORTEST.` → `NO CHRISTMAS. A DESERT.` → `THE FIRST LINE.`

segments.voice: Mark, chapter one, verse one. In the old English: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole verse. It's a title, and a door. Start with gospel: good news. Mark's Greek word is euangelion, and it wasn't a church word yet. Historians point to Roman-era inscriptions that use it for public announcements: a victory won, news about an emperor, news that changes the day for everyone who hears it. Mark takes that word and puts it on a builder from Galilee. Now the shape, so you know the mountain ahead. First, Galilee: a man baptized in a river, fishermen dropping their nets, healings, arguments, and the stories he told. A word Mark uses again and again here is straightway. Immediately. Everything happens fast. Then, right in the middle, the turning point. Jesus asks his friends: who do you say that I am? And from there the road turns toward Jerusalem. The last third of the book is one week: the entry into the city, the table and the bread, the cross, and the empty tomb, where the women run away, afraid. Which brings us back to the book's first word. Beginning. Some readers notice that Mark calls all of it, the whole book, just the beginning. As if the good news isn't finished when the book ends. As if the reader is supposed to pick it up from there.

segments.voice: Last sit of the camp. Sit, and breathe, the way you did on day one, when the first word was communion, a meal that remembers. Now let one word from these three weeks come back to you on its own. Don't pick it. Let it arrive. Grace, maybe. Or the stone already moved. Or small is enough. Hold it for a few breaths. Then ask, gently: where does this start for me? If you pray, you can offer that word back as your prayer, with an amen. If you don't, just hold it, and let it be a beginning.
